items.title: Olfactory function in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and its association with disease activity: a cross-sectional case-control study.
items.abstract: The aim of this study was to evaluate odor identification and odor threshold in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, compare these measures with those of healthy controls, and investigate their associations with disease activity. This cross-sectional case-control study with prospective participant recruitment included patients with rheumatoid arthritis and age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Odor identification (OI) was assessed using the 12-item Rapid Sniffin' Sticks test, and odor threshold (OT) was assessed using the modified CCCRC n-butanol test. Disease duration, disease activity scores, and inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein (CRP), were recorded. Associations between olfactory measures and disease-related parameters were analyzed. The distribution of odor threshold categories differed significantly between groups (p < 0.001), with higher proportions of anosmia and hyposmia in patients with rheumatoid arthritis than in healthy controls. Odor identification scores did not differ significantly between groups. No statistically significant associations were observed between OT categories or OI scores and disease duration, disease activity scores, or CRP levels. OI scores were higher among methotrexate users than non-users, whereas OT category distribution did not differ significantly according to methotrexate use. Neither olfactory measure was significantly associated with corticosteroid use. Rheumatoid arthritis was associated with an altered distribution of odor threshold categories, whereas odor identification scores did not differ significantly between groups. No statistically significant associations were observed between the olfactory measures and disease activity, disease duration, or CRP levels. These findings do not establish causality or independence from potential confounders. III. Key Points • Patients with rheumatoid arthritis had higher proportions of anosmia and hyposmia than healthy controls. • Odor identification scores did not differ significantly between patients with rheumatoid arthritis and healthy controls. • No statistically significant associations were observed between odor threshold categories or odor identification scores and disease activity, disease duration, or CRP levels. • Rheumatoid arthritis was associated with an altered distribution of odor threshold categories; the independence and causal nature of this association remain to be established.

items.title: Impact of radiographic damage on health-related outcomes across rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and hand osteoarthritis: a comparative analysis of disease burden.
items.abstract: To evaluate the comparative impact of radiographic joint damage on hand functions, objective grip strength, and quality of life across patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), psoriatic arthritis (PsA), and hand osteoarthritis (OA). This cross-sectional study included patients with RA (n = 50), PsA (n = 40), and hand OA (n = 40). Objective grip strength was measured using a calibrated JAMAR hydraulic dynamometer. Radiographic damage was assessed using the modified Total Sharp Score (mTSS) for inflammatory cohorts and the Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) scale for hand OA. Functional status and psychosocial impact were evaluated through Duruöz Hand Index (DHI), Quick Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder, and Hand (QuickDASH) questionnaire, Health Assessment Questionnaire (HAQ), and the Short Form-36 (SF-36) Health Survey scales. Spearman correlation analyses and adjusted multivariable linear regression models were performed to evaluate the relationship between radiographic damage and functional outcomes. Despite marked differences in disease duration, radiographic damage, and treatment profiles, objectively measured grip strength and patient-reported hand disability did not differ significantly among the three disease groups (all p > 0.05). In unadjusted analyses, greater radiographic damage was associated with lower grip strength in PsA (r = - 0.405, 95% CI - 0.637 to - 0.107), but not with QuickDASH or DHI; no significant associations between radiographic damage and these functional outcomes were observed in RA or hand OA. After multivariable adjustment, high radiographic damage remained associated with lower grip strength in PsA (β = - 9.02, 95% CI - 17.19 to - 0.85), but was not associated with QuickDASH or DHI. Disease activity was most strongly associated with functional outcomes in RA, whereas radiographic severity was not independently associated with grip strength or patient-reported hand function in hand OA. Grip strength was inversely correlated with hand-specific patient-reported outcomes across all disease groups. Although patients with RA, PsA, and hand OA experience comparable levels of hand dysfunction, the factors associated with functional impairment differ according to disease phenotype. Structural damage appears to have a greater influence on objective hand performance in PsA, whereas disease activity predominates in RA and radiographic severity alone does not explain disability in hand OA. These findings highlight the importance of disease-specific interpretation of structural damage and support comprehensive functional assessment in patients with inflammatory and degenerative hand arthritis. Key Points • Patients with RA, psoriatic arthritis, and hand OA exhibited comparable levels of objectively measured grip strength and patient-reported hand disability despite substantial differences in disease duration and radiographic severity. • Multivariable analyses demonstrated disease-specific determinants of functional impairment: radiographic damage was independently associated with reduced grip strength only in psoriatic arthritis, whereas disease activity was the principal factor associated with functional outcomes in RA and radiographic severity alone did not explain disability in hand OA. • Functional impairment in hand OA cannot be explained solely by structural radiographic changes, underscoring the need for comprehensive functional assessment beyond conventional imaging findings.

items.title: Coexistence of systemic lupus erythematosus and IgG4-related disease: a case report and literature review.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a chronic multisystem autoimmune disease with diverse clinical and serological manifestations. IgG4-related disease (IgG4-RD) is a systemic fibroinflammatory condition characterized by mass-forming lesions, dense IgG4-positive plasma cell infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis. Although rare, cases of SLE coexisting with IgG4-RD have been reported. We report a 44-year-old woman with a 15-year history of SLE with serositis, articular, and mucocutaneous involvement, who developed a painless mass in the left submandibular gland. Histopathological evaluation revealed dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration, storiform fibrosis, and obliterative phlebitis, with 97 IgG4 + plasma cells per high-power field and an IgG4/IgG ratio of 63%. Serum IgG4 was mildly elevated and was considered supportive rather than diagnostic. These findings supported a diagnosis of IgG4-RD. A literature review identified nine cases of SLE/IgG4-RD overlap; in most cases, the diagnoses of SLE and IgG4-RD were established concomitantly, whereas only a single report described IgG4-RD developing subsequent to SLE. In conclusion, the coexistence of SLE and IgG4-RD is possible. Recognition of this overlap is essential for individualized treatment strategies targeting both conditions. Key Points • IgG4-related disease can develop in patients with long-standing, established systemic lupus erythematosus.. • Non-fulfillment of the 2019 ACR/EULAR IgG4-RD classifi cation criteria, driven by SLE-associated serological exclusions, should not be used to exclude clinicopathologically confirmed coexistence. • Elevated serum IgG4 or IgG4+ plasma cells alone are insufficient to diagnose IgG4-RD in SLE; histopathology, quantitative immunostaining, and exclusion of mimickers are required. • None of the nine published SLE/IgG4-RD overlap cases fulfilled the IgG4-RD classification criteria.

items.title: Disease activity and patient-perceived health: associations with the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) in a large multicenter systemic lupus erythematosus cohort.
items.abstract: We aimed to evaluate the relationship between disease activity and the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) and to identify clinical and socio-demographic factors associated with PASS in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). We analyzed data from the Spanish multicenter SLE registry (RELESSER). PASS was self-reported. Disease activity was assessed using SLEDAI-2K and targeted disease activity states (DORIS remission and LLDAS). Collected variables included socio-demographic factors (age, sex, employment, educational attainment), fibromyalgia, organ damage (SDI), current therapies and the Lupus Impact Tracker (LIT). Associations with PASS were analyzed for each disease activity state measure by univariable and multivariable logistic regression. A subgroup analysis was performed in patients in DORIS remission. 72% of patients (n=1249) reported being in PASS. Lower SLEDAI-2K, DORIS remission and LLDAS were independently associated with being in PASS. Higher education level and being employed were positively associated, while female sex and fibromyalgia were negatively associated with PASS. After including LIT items in the models, DORIS remission and LLDAS remained associated, while pain, fatigue-related limitations and anxiety showed the strongest associations. Among patients in DORIS remission, 20% were not in PASS, with female sex, fibromyalgia, pain, fatigue-related limitations and anxiety remaining independent barriers. DORIS remission and LLDAS are associated with PASS, supporting their relevance as treatment targets from the patient's perspective. Pain, fatigue and anxiety hinder many patients with SLE from achieving satisfactory health beyond disease remission. One in five patients in remission is still not in PASS. PASS assessment may help capture unmet needs in SLE management.

items.title: Threshold of Hydroxychloroquine Dose Reduction Associated with Flare in Quiescent Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
items.abstract: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ) is recommended for nearly all patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) unless contraindicated. However, concerns regarding long-term toxicity have led to increasing consideration of HCQ dose reduction or discontinuation. The threshold of HCQ dose reduction in clinically quiescent SLE remain unclear. This retrospective cohort included 381 patients with SLE in clinical remission (cSLEDAI-2K=0, prednisolone ≤5 mg/day, ongoing HCQ). The primary outcome was SLE flare, defined as ≥1-point increase in clinical SLEDAI-2K or treatment escalation. HCQ dose reduction during follow-up was evaluated using adjusted Cox proportional hazards models (aHR) for time-to-flare and adjusted logistic regression for flare occurrence (aOR). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis identified the reduction threshold. Over a median follow-up of 1.38 years, 52.5% developed flares. HCQ discontinuation was associated with increased flare risk (aHR 1.80, 95% CI 1.17-2.75; aOR 5.60, 95% CI 2.47-12.71). A ≥75% reduction was similarly associated with higher flare risk (aHR 1.53, 95% CI 1.02-2.30; aOR 4.40, 95% CI 2.17-8.92), whereas lesser reductions were not. Each 10% dose reduction showed a dose-response relationship in logistic analysis (aOR 1.13, 95% CI 1.06-1.21). ROC analysis identified a 74.7% reduction as an exploratory threshold for HCQ dose reduction (AUC 0.55). In clinically quiescent SLE, HCQ discontinuation and substantial dose reduction (≥75%) are associated with increased flare risk. These findings support cautious HCQ tapering and avoidance of marked dose reduction.

items.title: Effects of a Smartphone-Enabled, Physician-Supervised Treat-to-Target Model for Gout Management: A 12-Month Randomized Controlled Trial.
items.abstract: To evaluate whether an integrated, smartphone-enabled, physician-supervised treat-to-target (T2T) care model improves serum urate (SUA) target attainment compared with usual care, and to explore its effects on gout flares and systemic metabolic parameters. This 12-month, single-center, open-label, superiority randomized controlled trial enrolled 280 men with gout. Participants were randomized (1:1) to an integrated digitally supported care model (the "1CARE" platform combining automated behavioral reminders, tiered education, remote SUA monitoring, and weekly physician review) or Usual Care. The primary outcome was the proportion of patients achieving serum urate (SUA) <360μmol/L. Secondary outcomes included gout flares and metabolic parameters. At 12 months, 85.0% (119/140) of participants in the App-Led group achieved the primary therapeutic target of SUA<360μmol/L, compared with 48.6% (68/140) in the Usual Care group (risk ratio 1.75 [95% CI 1.46 to 2.10]; P < 0.0001). The App-Led Care group also showed a significantly lower annualized gout flare frequency (0.02 vs 0.10 flares/year; P < 0.01). Exploratory metabolic outcomes favored the App-Led Care group, with greater reductions in fasting plasma glucose, HbA1c, total cholesterol, and LDL cholesterol (all P < 0.05), alongside higher medication adherence. Adverse event rates were comparable between the two groups. An integrated, physician-supervised, digitally supported T2T care model significantly improved SUA target attainment and reduced gout flares compared with usual care over 12 months. Multi-center trials will be needed to fully evaluate the generalizability, cost-effectiveness, and optimal configuration of this approach.

items.title: Differentiation and Pathological Significance of Tissue-Resident Memory-Like CD8 + T Cells in Systemic Lupus Erythematosus.
items.abstract: Tissue-resident memory T (T RM ) cells have been implicated in organ-specific immune pathology; however, the pathological relevance of T RM -like CD8 + T cells in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) remains unclear. We investigated their differentiation mechanisms and pathological significance in SLE, including associations with disease activity and organ involvement. Peripheral blood samples from 30 treatment-naïve patients with SLE, 40 patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), and 30 healthy donors (HDs) were analyzed by flow cytometry. Renal biopsy specimens from 20 patients with SLE were examined by immunofluorescence. Naïve CD8 + T cells from HDs were stimulated with cytokines to induce T RM -like differentiation, followed by phenotypic, functional, transcriptional, and metabolic analyses. The effects of Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors were assessed. Circulating CD8 + CD69 + CD103 + T RM -like cells were more frequent in SLE than in RA and HDs (P=0.022 and P<0.001, respectively) and correlated with anti-dsDNA antibodies (rs=0.468, P=0.016) and CH50 (rs=-0.397, P=0.045). Patients with active kidney involvement (renal BILAG A/B; n=17) had higher T RM -like cell proportions than those without active kidney involvement (n=13; P<0.05). CD3 + CD103 + cells in renal lesions expressed granzyme B or interferon-γ. Patients with baseline T RM -like cell proportions ≥0.40% had higher urine protein-to-creatinine ratios and SELENA-SLEDAI scores at week 24 (both P<0.05). IL-15 plus TGF-β1 induced T RM -like differentiation with effector, transcriptional, survival, and metabolic features, whereas JAK inhibition suppressed differentiation and granzyme B expression. Circulating T RM -like CD8 + T cells were associated with SLE activity and kidney involvement. IL-15/TGF-β1-dependent differentiation partly involved JAK/STAT signaling, supporting further evaluation as a biomarker and therapeutic target.

items.title: Evaluation of fluorescein staining with the yellow filter in the diagnosis of Sjögren disease in Japan.
items.abstract: Sjögren disease (SjD) requires ocular surface assessment during diagnostic evaluation. In Japan, the 1999 revised Japanese Ministry of Health criteria include the van Bijsterveld score based on the Rose Bengal test; however, this test is rarely performed in current clinical practice. Although fluorescein staining with the yellow filter is widely used as an alternative method, its performance for suspected SjD remains unclear. To clinically evaluate this method, this multicenter retrospective study included 400 patients who underwent fluorescein staining with the yellow filter for suspected SjD between 2010 and 2024. Expert clinical diagnosis served as the reference diagnosis, with 322 being diagnosed with SjD and 78 classified as non-SjD. At a cutoff value ≥3 for the van Bijsterveld score using fluorescein staining with the yellow filter, sensitivity was 48.4% and specificity 84.6%, with a positive predictive value of 92.9%. At a cutoff value ≥4, sensitivity was 32.6% and specificity 93.6%, with a positive predictive value of 95.5%. After replacing the Rose Bengal test in the 1999 criteria with fluorescein staining with the yellow filter, the modified criteria showed 86.6% sensitivity, 93.6% specificity, and 88.0% accuracy. Fluorescein staining with the yellow filter may be a practical ocular assessment method for suspected SjD.

items.title: Prevalence and clinical associations of age-related clonal hematopoiesis in systemic sclerosis.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is an autoimmune disease involving both innate and adaptive immunity, characterized by progressive organ fibrosis. Age-related clonal hematopoiesis (ARCH) results from somatic mutations in hematopoietic progenitors and is increasingly implicated in inflammation and autoimmunity. We aimed to assess the prevalence of ARCH in patients with SSc and its association with disease characteristics. Targeted myeloid next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed in 196 patients with SSc and 392 age- and gender-matched individuals without SSc and referred for NGS without a final diagnosis myelodysplastic syndrome. Variants with variant allele frequency (VAF) ≥0.8% were considered for ARCH analysis. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) was defined as ARCH with a VAF ≥2%. The prevalence of ARCH and CHIP was similar between SSc patients and the control group: 32.7% vs. 37.2% (p = 0.25) and 23.5% vs. 28.8% (p = 0.15), respectively. Among patients with SSc, ARCH was associated with higher NT-proBNP levels and higher prevalence of progressive interstitial lung disease (ILD) (39.1% versus 15.7%, p = 0.026), pulmonary hypertension (23.4% vs. 11.4%, p = 0.028), valvular heart disease (23.4% vs. 11.4%, p = 0.028), anti-centromere antibodies (65.1% versus 49.6%, p = 0.043) in our cohort. After adjustment to age and gender, only NT-proBNP levels remain significantly higher in SSc patients with ARCH. These associations were not observed when restricting the analysis to CHIP except for valvular heart disease (26.1% vs. 11.4%, p = 0.019) and higher NT proBNP levels. The prevalence of ARCH and CHIP was 32.7% and 23.5% respectively in our cohort of patients with SSc Presence of ARCH was associated with more severe pulmonary involvement, a higher frequency of pulmonary hypertension, valvular heart disease and anti-centromere antibodies. After adjustement to age and sex, ARCH was associate with a higher NT-pro BNP levels.

items.title: Large vessel giant cell arteritis in remission: Is imaging useful as predictor for relapses?
items.abstract: To evaluate whether vasculitic findings (VF) on [¹⁸F] fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at treatment stop (TS) are associated with relapse in patients with large vessel giant cell arteritis (LV-GCA), and to explore the association between PET/CT-based polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) findings and relapse. LV-GCA patients included in our local GCA cohort BARK who discontinued treatment in remission and underwent PET/CT and/or MRI within ±4 months of TS were included. VF were defined using standardized criteria. Periarticular inflammation in PET/CT was scored by the Leuven score and a cut-off ≥12 was considered positive. Patients were followed for relapse. Statistics used Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression. VF at TS were observed in 54% of patients (25/46), including 47% of MRIs (15/32), 50% of PET/CTs (14/28), and 4/14 positive on both modalities. During follow-up, 48% (22/46) of patients relapsed in median 4.7 months after TS (82% minor, 18% major relapses). Overall, VF at TS was not associated with relapse (p = 0.1). PET/CT findings, including SUV segment/liver ratio and a modified PETVAS were not predictive for relapse (p ≥ 0.6). Absence of VF in MRI at TS was associated with relapse (p = 0.005). Six patients had positive Leuven score at TS and all relapsed (HR 5.35, 95% CI 1.70-16.83, p = 0.004). Vascular imaging at TS did not predict relapse in our cohort. There is a signal pointing towards a potential association of periarticular inflammation in PET/CT at TS to subsequent relapses, that warrants further validation.

items.title: Krebs Von Den Lungen-6 as a biomarker for lung disease activity and diagnosis in systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis.
items.abstract: Children with systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis (sJIA) and lung disease (LD) are at increased risk of serious complications and premature mortality, making early detection and intervention critical. Krebs von den Lungen 6 (KL-6) is a blood-based biomarker for interstitial lung disease in adults; however, its role in pediatric LD is unclear. This study evaluates KL-6 as a discriminatory and disease activity biomarker for sJIA-LD. Thirty-two patients with sJIA-LD were enrolled through the Childhood Arthritis and Research Alliance (CARRA) Registry. Comparators included sJIA patients without LD, children with primary pulmonary alveolar proteinosis (PAP), and healthy control children. Median KL-6 levels were significantly higher in sJIA-LD (596.3 U/mL [IQR 273.5-5,896.3]) compared to sJIA without LD (193.0 U/mL [151.0-252.0], p < 0.0001) and healthy controls (171.9 U/mL [89.7-224.3], p = 0.001), with no difference versus PAP (596.3 vs. 1429.9, p = 0.30). A cut-off of 259.5 U/mL yielded 81.3% sensitivity and 80.9% specificity for LD (AUC 0.856, p < 0.0001). At 371.5 U/mL, specificity reached 100% with 68.7% sensitivity and 100% positive predictive value. SJIA-LD features associated with higher median KL-6 levels included oxygen requirement, abnormal pulse oximeter (<90%), and abnormal chest radiographs. KL-6 strongly correlated with physician global assessment of lung disease but not with markers of systemic inflammation or macrophage activation syndrome. KL-6 is a useful biomarker for discriminating LD and evaluating disease activity in sJIA-LD. Future efforts should focus on the utility of KL-6 for monitoring disease progression, treatment response, and predicting long-term disease trajectories.

items.title: Obinutuzumab in systemic sclerosis: a multicentre retrospective case series.
items.abstract: To describe a real-life case series of patients with systemic sclerosis (SSc) treated with obinutuzumab (OBZ), a next-generation glycoengineered type II anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, reporting for the first time its use in SSc. We retrospectively collected clinical, laboratory, and instrumental data from five patients with SSc treated with OBZ. All patients were multi-refractory and previously treated by Rituximab (RTX), stopped in 4/5 cases because of allergic reactions. We reported safety data, immunological changes and clinical effectiveness. OBZ was administered at 1g on days 0 and 15, with maintenance infusions every 5-6 months. Patients were refractory to a median of five prior immunosuppressive therapies. At a median follow-up of 12 months, OBZ was well tolerated, without allergic cross-reaction or serious adverse events. Complete peripheral CD19+ B-cell depletion was achieved in all patients. Gamma-globulin levels decreased from a median of 11.7 to 8.8 g/L. Skin fibrosis improved, with median mRSS decreasing from 27 (range 4-31) to 8 (range 0-23). Articular remission was achieved in all assessable patients. Across 3 SSc-interstitial lung disease patients, lung parenchymal disease remained stable on functional assessment and imaging. Corticosteroid doses were reduced or stabilised in all patients, from a median of 10 mg (range 0-20) to 5 mg (range 0-10) per day. OBZ may represent a valuable therapeutic option in SSc, particularly in patients with RTX intolerance or inadequate response. Meaningful clinical benefit was observed even in advanced, non-inflammatory phenotypes; whether deeper, tissue-level B-cell depletion contributes to this benefit remains a hypothesis to be investigated prospectively.

items.title: FSTL1 and NLRP3 Inflammasome Activation in Lupus Nephritis: A Mesenchyme-to-Macrophage Hypothesis.
items.abstract: Lupus nephritis (LN) is a major cause of morbidity in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), and current therapies often fail to prevent end-stage renal disease. Follistatin-like protein 1 (FSTL1), a mesenchymal/stromal-derived glycoprotein, is implicated in renal inflammation. To synthesize evidence for a proposed FSTL1-driven NLRP3 inflammasome axis in LN and to identify gaps relevant to biomarker development and targeted therapy. We examine the hypothesis that stromal/tubular FSTL1 is internalized by macrophages and activates NLRP3 via dual signals: mitochondrial ATP production (activation) and transcriptional upregulation of Nlrp3/pro-caspase-1 (priming), with resulting IL-1β amplifying tubulointerstitial inflammation and fibrosis. We assess evidence that FSTL1 is elevated in SLE sera, whereas direct LN kidney evidence is limited to one Chinese-language immunohistochemical study and NLRP3 colocalization has not been demonstrated in biopsy-proven LN; CKD and UUO models suggest FSTL1 may be present in LN kidney but this remains untested. We also discuss post-translational modifications, extracellular vesicle shuttling, and immunometabolism as unexplored determinants of context-dependent FSTL1 behavior. The proposed mesenchyme/stroma-to-macrophage axis may offer new opportunities for LN biomarkers and targeted therapy, but current evidence is largely indirect and should be interpreted as a mechanistic framework requiring rigorous translational validation.

items.title: Methotrexate multivesicular liposome sustained alleviates rheumatoid arthritis in rats.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic inflammatory disease that can cause progressive joint damage. Although methotrexate (MTX) is a first-line treatment for RA, conventional administration may cause systemic adverse effects, highlighting the need for sustained local drug delivery. This study aimed to develop MTX-loaded multivesicular liposomes (MTX-MVLs) for sustained intra-articular delivery and improved RA treatment. MTX-MVLs were prepared using a double-emulsion method and optimized for formulation and process parameters. Their physicochemical properties, in vitro drug release, therapeutic efficacy, joint retention, and systemic safety were evaluated. The optimized MTX-MVLs exhibited high drug encapsulation efficiency and sustained drug release. In an adjuvant-induced arthritis rat model, a single weekly intra-articular injection of MTX-MVLs achieved therapeutic efficacy comparable to biweekly injections of free MTX, while reducing joint swelling and pro-inflammatory cytokine levels. MTX-MVLs also demonstrated prolonged joint retention and a favorable organ safety profile. These findings suggest that MTX-MVLs may provide a promising sustained-release platform for local MTX delivery and warrant further investigation for RA treatment.

items.title: ALDH4A1 and anti-ALDH4A1 emerge as a novel antigenic axis linked to atherosclerosis in rheumatoid arthritis.
items.abstract: Cardiovascular risk excess in rheumatoid arthritis (RA) cannot be explained by traditional risk factors alone. Recent experimental data have identified ALDH4A1 as a mitochondrial self-antigen implicated in atherosclerosis, yet its clinical significance in human autoimmunity remains unexplored. We aimed to characterize ALDH4A1 and anti-ALDH4A1 antibody levels in early RA, and evaluate their associations with atherosclerosis burden and lipoprotein traits. ALDH4A1 and anti-ALDH4A1 antibodies (IgM, IgG, IgA, and IgG subclasses) were measured in early RA (n = 82), clinically suspect arthralgia (n = 14), healthy controls (n = 70), and a validation cohort of established RA. A prospective cohort (n = 13) explored therapeutic modulation under TNF blockade. Associations with atherosclerosis burden, lipid/lipoprotein profiles, oxylipin signatures, proteomics, and cell-free DNA were assessed. ALDH4A1 serum levels were associated with apoptotic-related proteomic pathways, cell-free DNA and lipidomic signatures in early RA. Reduced anti-ALDH4A1 antibodies were found, although divergent patters were noted across isotypes. These differences were confirmed in a validation cohort. IgG (predominantly IgG3) anti-ALDH4A1 correlated with favourable lipoprotein traits and cardiometabolic risk factors. Increased ALDH4A1 and reduced IgM/IgG anti-ALDH4A1 antibodies independently predicted atherosclerosis and improved risk stratification beyond mSCORE, most notably for IgG. ALDH4A1 tracked with TNF dynamics under TNF blockade, whereas increases in IgG antibodies occurred in responders and paralleled changes in lipoprotein features. The ALDH4A1/anti-ALDH4A1 axis emerges as a novel player bridging lipid disturbances and atherosclerosis along the whole RA continuum, hence highlighting the involvement of mitochondrial targets. These components hold promise as functional players, clinical tools and therapeutic targets.

items.title: Tumoral Calcium Pyrophosphate Deposition in the Glenohumeral Joint: A Case Report.
items.abstract: A 75-year-old male patient presented with long-standing pain and swelling in the shoulder. Radiographic evaluations revealed a large, calcified mass posterior to the humeral head, without apparent bone erosion or destruction. Magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an intra-articular mass-like lesion in the glenohumeral joint without apparent extension into the adjacent bone or surrounding soft tissues. Because the lesion appeared nonaggressive on imaging, a benign calcified intra-articular lesion was initially considered. Open and arthroscopy-assisted excision of the lesion was performed because of severe pain and restricted range of motion. Pathological examination demonstrated abundant crystalline deposits with angular and elongated morphology, consistent with calcium pyrophosphate deposition disease, leading to the diagnosis of tophaceous pseudogout. Two years after the surgery, radiography showed mild enlargement of the residual calcific deposits, although the patient remained asymptomatic. Tophaceous pseudogout of the glenohumeral joint is rare and may mimic neoplastic lesions on imaging; therefore, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of calcified masses in the shoulder.

items.title: Advanced practice nursing and nurse-led models in systemic lupus erythematosus: A patient organisation-informed narrative review.
items.abstract: ObjectiveTo synthesise how nurse-led models and advanced nursing practice are described in systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) care and to interpret reported outcomes in light of priorities identified through consultation with patient organisations.MethodsWe conducted a patient organisation-informed narrative review. Two patient organisations contributed via targeted consultations to refine the review question, identify priority outcomes, and support interpretation. We searched three databases from inception to January 2026 for peer-reviewed articles describing nurse-led interventions, service models, or advanced nursing roles involving people with SLE. Two reviewers screened records, extracted data, and synthesized findings using thematic analysis.ResultsOf 376 records, nine articles published between 2016 and 2025 were included; none originated from Africa or Latin America, and only one addressed pediatric care. Nurse-led activity was most often delivered in outpatient and hybrid (in-person/telephone) formats. Five main themes were synthesised: (i) Care coordination and continuity as the "backbone"; (ii) Education and counselling to strengthen self-management and self-efficacy; (iii) Symptom and lifestyle management as central outcomes; (iv) Psychosocial needs and social determinants as part of care; and (v) Advanced competence, training, and variable "visibility" of nursing roles.ConclusionSLE services should formalise advanced rheumatology nursing roles and nurse-led models as part of routine care, with clear governance and escalation processes. Future research should standardise role descriptions and outcomes and evaluate scalable nurse-led models on patient-centred, service, and equity endpoints.

items.title: Subclinical Retinal Perfusion Changes in Patients with Takayasu Arteritis.
items.abstract: To investigate subclinical ocular alterations in patients with Takayasu arteritis (TA) without Takayasu retinopathy (TR) using optical coherence tomography (OCT) and OCT-angiography (OCTA). In this cross-sectional study, 53 TA patients fulfilling the 2022 EULAR criteria and 53 age- and sex-matched controls underwent comprehensive ophthalmologic evaluation, including multimodal imaging. Structural parameters (retinal and choroidal thickness) and vascular parameters [foveal avascular zone (FAZ), vessel density of superficial (SCP) and deep (DCP) capillary plexuses, and choriocapillaris perfusion] were quantified. Associations between vascular metrics and systemic manifestations were analyzed. No patient showed clinical signs of TR. Compared with controls, TA patients had significantly greater subfoveal choroidal thickness (361 ± 64 μm vs 307 ± 70 μm, p  < 0.001) and FAZ area (0.38 ± 0.19 mm 2 vs 0.30 ± 0.11 mm 2 , p  = 0.044) and reduced SCP vessel density (35.09 ± 2.98% vs 36.75 ± 2.43%, p  = 0.002). DCP vessel density and choriocapillaris perfusion did not differ significantly. In exploratory analyses, larger FAZ area was associated with arthritis and dizziness, while associations with headache, carotid artery involvement and limb claudication did not reach statistical significance. Choroidal thickness was greater in patients receiving glucocorticoids. TA patients without TR showed subclinical retinal and choroidal alterations, namely lower SCP vessel density, a larger FAZ, and greater subfoveal choroidal thickness than matched controls. These cross-sectional findings indicate associations rather than causal relationships, and their clinical relevance requires confirmation in larger longitudinal studies. OCTA may help detect subclinical ocular involvement in TA, but its role as a biomarker remains to be established.

items.title: EXPRESS: Calprotectin in Systemic Sclerosis: Pathogenic Roles and Emerging Biomarker Potential.
items.abstract: Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a complex autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by microvascular injury, immune dysregulation, and progressive fibrosis affecting the skin and multiple internal organs. Growing evidence suggests that calprotectin, a heterodimeric calcium-binding protein composed of S100A8 and S100A9, may contribute to the inflammatory processes involved in SSc pathogenesis. Increased calprotectin levels have been reported in multiple biological compartments of SSc patients, including bronchoalveolar lavage fluid, plasma, feces, skin, and saliva, and have been associated with systemic inflammatory activity and specific organ manifestations. Mechanistically, calprotectin functions as a damage-associated molecular pattern and may amplify inflammatory signaling through Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) and receptor for advanced glycation end-products (RAGE) pathways, potentially contributing to endothelial dysfunction, immune activation, and fibroblast-mediated fibrotic responses. Current evidence indicates that calprotectin may be involved in key clinical manifestations of SSc, particularly interstitial lung disease and gastrointestinal involvement, although its precise pathogenic role and clinical significance remain incompletely defined. This review summarizes current research on the biological characteristics of calprotectin in SSc, its distribution across different biological sources, and its potential value as a non-invasive biomarker candidate for assessing disease activity, organ involvement, and treatment response, while highlighting current limitations and future research directions.

items.title: Can baseline HALP score predict clinical outcomes and biologic therapy need in patients with rheumatoid arthritis?
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by inflammation and systemic effects, with biomarkers used to assess disease burden. The HALP score, based on hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte, and platelet levels, is being studied as a potential indicator of inflammation and nutrition. This study aimed to evaluate whether the baseline HALP score was associated with subsequent disease activity and treatment patterns in patients with rheumatoid arthritis, particularly biologic therapy use. This cross-sectional study included 130 RA patients grouped by disease activity and treatment regimen (DMARDs only, biologics only, combination therapy). HALP scores were calculated and analyzed alongside clinical variables using Mann-Whitney U, ANOVA, and correlation analyses. The mean HALP score was significantly higher in male patients compared to females ( p  = 0.010). No statistically significant associations were found between HALP scores and age, age at diagnosis, or disease duration. Patients on DMARDs alone showed higher disease activity than those on biologics or combination therapy ( p  = 0.018). However, HALP scores did not correlate significantly with DAS28 ( p  = 0.949) or treatment type ( p  = 0.767). While the HALP score showed gender-based differences and may reflect certain inflammatory or nutritional aspects, baseline HALP score was not significantly associated with subsequent disease activity or current treatment patterns in this cohort. However, further prospective studies using contemporaneous laboratory and clinical assessments are required to determine its independent clinical utility in rheumatoid arthritis.

items.title: The altered T cell landscape in systemic sclerosis patients is characterized by dysfunctional type 1 immunity.
items.abstract: T cells in patients with chronic autoimmunity show features of dysfunction. However, the functionally defined T cell subsets that are affected by these changes remain poorly characterized. Here, we sought to reveal aberrations in the composition, phenotype, and function of canonical T cell subsets in the blood of systemic sclerosis (SSc) patients compared with healthy subjects and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) patients. Therefore, we developed a novel multidimensional flow-cytometry panel to simultaneously detect lineage-defining transcription factors, co-inhibitory receptors and other functional markers to characterize T cell subsets without in vitro restimulation. We compared T cell landscapes in SSc and SLE patients, and healthy subjects, using opt-SNE (optimized t-distributed stochastic neighbor embedding) and PhenoGraph algorithms. The data show altered distribution and aberrant functional states of transcription factor-defined T cell subsets in patients with autoimmunity, with shared and unique features between diseases and their subtypes. Strikingly, SSc and SLE patients showed deficiencies in subsets of CD8+ and CD4-CD8- T cells that expressed T-bet, which is critical for IFN-γ-dependent type 1 immunity. Moreover, TIGIT+Foxp3+ regulatory T cells, which suppress T helper 1 responses, were increased in diffuse cutaneous SSc and SLE patients. Functionally, T cells from SSc patients produced less IFN-γ, a cytokine that suppresses profibrotic gene expression in fibroblasts, as we demonstrate by transcriptomic analysis. Our study supports a model in which IFN-γ opposes canonical fibrotic gene programs in fibroblasts, and deficiencies in the IFN-γ-producing T cell compartment in SSc patients therefore may contribute to chronic fibrosis development. Aberrant T cell subsets in SSc and SLE represent targets for corrective immunotherapy.

items.title: Low-Titre ANA Late-Onset Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Presenting With Pleural Effusion and Markedly Elevated Pleural Adenosine Deaminase Mimicking Tuberculous Pleuritis.
items.abstract: Pleural effusion with markedly elevated adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels is commonly associated with tuberculous pleuritis but may occur in other conditions. We report a case of low-titre ANA late-onset systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) presenting with pleural effusion and markedly elevated ADA levels mimicking tuberculosis. A 78-year-old man with pneumoconiosis presented with fever, cough, and progressive pleural effusion. Pleural fluid analysis revealed lymphocyte-predominant exudative effusion with markedly elevated ADA levels. Tuberculous pleuritis was initially suspected, but microbiological tests were negative. The patient developed thrombocytopenia, renal dysfunction, and altered consciousness. Immunological findings showed hypocomplementemia and elevated anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies despite low-titre ANA. Corticosteroid therapy led to rapid improvement, confirming the diagnosis of late-onset SLE. Clinicians should consider autoimmune diseases when tuberculosis is not microbiologically confirmed.

items.title: Risk Factors and Subtype-Specific Prediction Models for Arterial versus Venous Thrombotic Events in Chinese Patients with Lupus Nephritis: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Autoimmune diseases heighten thrombosis risk, yet large-scale studies that systematically profile risk factors while simultaneously distinguishing arterial from venous events in lupus nephritis (LN) remain lacking. This study aimed to determine the incidence and arterial-venous distribution of thrombosis in LN, identify independent risk factors for overall, arterial, and venous thrombosis, and construct separate prediction models for each subtype. This single-center retrospective study included 348 patients with biopsy-confirmed LN from 2017 to 2023. Over a median follow-up period of 4 years (with a maximum of 8 years), all thrombotic events were verified through imaging. Cox regression analysis was employed to identify independent risk factors, while time-dependent area under the curve (AUC) and Harrell's C-index were utilized to assess model discrimination. The overall incidence of thrombosis was 14.1% (49/348), with arterial events being more prevalent (55.1% arterial and 40.8% venous). Independent risk factors for overall thrombosis included age at diagnosis (HR=1.036, P <0.0001), hypertension (HR=2.097, P =0.011), smoking (HR=3.155, P <0.0001), and the positive lupus anticoagulant (LA) (HR=3.266, P <0.0001). Arterial thrombosis was independently associated with age, hypertension, smoking, and the Systemic Lupus Erythematosus Disease Activity Index (SLE-DAI), while venous thrombosis was associated with age and positive LA. The arterial model exhibited excellent discrimination (3-year AUC=0.909, C-index=0.884), whereas the venous model demonstrated moderate discrimination (3-year AUC=0.766, C-index=0.752). This study provides the first systematic characterization of thrombosis in Chinese LN patients with a specific focus on arterial-venous heterogeneity, and constructs separate risk prediction models. The arterial prediction model demonstrates excellent discriminative performance and may serve as a guide for thrombotic risk stratification. Venous prediction model demonstrated moderate discrimination. Both models rely on routinely available clinical variables. Routine LA screening, alongside standardized management of modifiable cardiovascular risk factors, should be incorporated into long-term thromboprophylaxis strategies for LN.

items.title: Breath molecular feature profiling with machine learning for noninvasive diagnosis of gout: a single-center case-control study.
items.abstract: Gout, a purine metabolism disorder with growing global prevalence, is currently diagnosed by ACR/EULAR criteria, yet complementary noninvasive tools remain limited. We evaluated whether breath molecular feature analysis could discriminate established gout patients from healthy controls. In this preliminary single-center study, breath samples were collected from 201 participants (99 established gout patients and 102 healthy controls). Breath molecular features were profiled by electrospray extraction ionization mass spectrometry (EESI-MS). Random forest machine-learning was applied to build classification models and identify discriminatory breath molecular features. Tongue-coating features and clinical characteristic were also compared between groups. EESI-MS profiling of exhaled breath identified 12 differential breath molecular features as candidate gout biomarkers. The putative urate dimer was significantly upregulated, whereas the other 11 ions were downregulated. The BreathGOUT model based on breath molecular features achieved an AUC of 0.999 (95% CI 0.997-1.000) by 5-fold stratified cross-validation, with accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity all reaching 0.990. Unimodal decomposition analysis confirmed that BreathGOUT retained an AUC of 0.999, indicating that breath molecular features provided discriminatory information complementary to that captured by clinical characteristics alone. The trimodal integrated model, BreathGOUT-Plus, also yielded an AUC of 0.999; although it did not further improve diagnostic performance, it enhanced robustness against short-term confounding influences. In this case-control setting, machine-learning analysis of breath molecular features reliably discriminated established gout from healthy states. The model demonstrated excellent discriminative power and identified candidate biomarkers. Multimodal fusion improved clinical robustness and interpretability across Western and traditional Chinese medicine dimensions. This proof-of-concept supports future multicenter studies incorporating asymptomatic hyperuricemia, first-presentation arthritis, and other arthritides to assess broader clinical applicability.

items.title: Extracapsular and joint-dominant hand and wrist MRI patterns in psoriatic and rheumatoid arthritis: an exploratory case-control study.
items.abstract: Psoriatic arthritis (PsA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) may present with overlapping hand and wrist symptoms, while their anatomical patterns of inflammation differ. To compare prespecified hand and wrist magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features between PsA and RA and to assess selected exploratory associations, discriminatory performance, anatomical distributions and reader reliability. This retrospective case-control study included 41 patients with PsA and 41 with RA who underwent clinically acquired 3.0-T hand or wrist MRI. Research MRI features were assigned retrospectively by readers blinded to the clinical diagnosis. Between-group comparisons used available-case denominators. Each adjusted model included one MRI feature together with age, sex and symptom duration; Firth bias-reduced logistic regression was used for the sparse vascular-like signal feature. Compared with RA, PsA had higher median scores for extracapsular soft tissue inflammation (7 vs. 2), periarthritis (8 vs. 4) and bead-like peritendinous effusion (1 vs. 0; all P <0.01). Study-defined prominent reticular vascular-like signal occurred in 35/41 patients with PsA and 2/41 with RA and showed a strong but imprecise adjusted association with PsA (odds ratio 85.02, 95% CI 15.07-479.83). RA had a higher median joint effusion score (5 vs. 2) and more frequent wrist synovitis (33/41 vs. 7/37) and wrist bone erosion (30/41 vs. 8/39; all P <0.01). Inter-reader coefficients ranged from 0.574 to 0.914 and intra-reader coefficients from 0.846 to 0.968. The historical screening denominator and formal composite disease activity scores could not be reconstructed; one clinically diagnosed RA case did not meet the retrospective classification threshold; treatment exposure differed between groups; distal interphalangeal and ulnocarpal coverage was incomplete; and external validation was not performed. In this exploratory cohort, extracapsular and enthesis-associated MRI findings favored PsA, whereas joint effusion and wrist synovitis or erosion favored RA. The study-defined vascular-like and bead-like features require independent validation before clinical use.

items.title: Phenotypic and immunological profile divergence between SLE-associated myelitis and SLE-NMOSD overlap syndrome: a retrospective case series.
items.abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus-associated myelitis (SLE-AM) is a devastating neuroimmunological complication. Increasing evidence suggests that myelitis occurring in patients with SLE is heterogeneous and may include non-overlap SLE-AM and SLE-neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) overlap syndrome. We aimed to describe the clinical, radiological, CSF inflammatory and systemic immunological profiles of patients with these conditions and to explore their potential therapeutic implications. We conducted a retrospective, single-center case series of six patients with SLE-associated myelitis treated at the First Affiliated Hospital of Dalian Medical University. Two patients were classified as having non-overlap SLE-AM and four as having SLE-NMOSD overlap syndrome according to clinical, radiological, and serological findings. Among the six patients, five were women and one was a man; Patients 1 and 2 had non-overlap SLE-AM, whereas Patients 3-6 had SLE-NMOSD overlap syndrome. In Patients 1 and 2, myelitis occurred concurrently with SLE onset and was accompanied by marked cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) inflammation, high anti-dsDNA antibody levels, and complement consumption. Patients 3-6 had more heterogeneous temporal courses and generally lower routine CSF inflammatory indices; serum AQP4-IgG was positive in Patients 4-6 and was not tested in Patient 3. Despite intensive immunosuppressive treatment, several patients had substantial residual neurological disability during follow-up. Notably, Patient 4 showed improvement in left-leg pain and remained clinically stable, with no recurrence over nearly 7 months of follow-up after inebilizumab treatment. Non-overlap SLE-AM and SLE-NMOSD overlap syndrome may show differing clinical and CSF profiles. Detailed serological and CSF characterization may help distinguish these clinical patterns and inform more individualized therapeutic strategies.

items.title: Case Report: Refractory childhood-onset takayasu arteritis with digital clubbing and extensive supra-aortic and lower-limb arterial disease.
items.abstract: Childhood-onset Takayasu arteritis is rare, and its early picture is often too vague to point at a large-vessel vasculitis. We report a 12-year-old girl who presented with 13 days of recurrent severe retrosternal chest pain and diffuse colicky abdominal pain, on a background of six months of exertional fatigue and painful swelling of the right fingertips, without fever, weight loss or night sweats. Examination showed bilateral digital clubbing, a right arm blood pressure below the 5th percentile with left arm and lower limb readings between the 50th and 90th percentiles, an absent right radial pulse, and weak brachial and right posterior tibial pulses. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 110 mm/h and C-reactive protein 82 to 93 mg/L. Computed tomography angiography showed mild concentric mural thickening of the aortic arch with severe stenosis of the right common and internal carotid arteries, near-occlusion of the right subclavian artery, moderate to severe brachiocephalic stenosis, moderate narrowing of the left common carotid and left subclavian arteries, and moderate stenosis of the right common and superficial femoral arteries. The abdominal aorta and its visceral branches were spared. She met the EULAR/PRINTO/PRES (Ankara 2008) classification criteria for childhood Takayasu arteritis, and the arterial distribution corresponds to Numano type IIa, together with peripheral lower-limb involvement that the Numano scheme does not cover. Disease progressed on intravenous methylprednisolone, oral prednisolone, methotrexate, aspirin and low-molecular-weight heparin, culminating in an 80% stenosis of the right common femoral artery. Adalimumab was started and later replaced by tocilizumab, after which the femoral peri-arterial inflammatory changes resolved on imaging and acute-phase reactants normalized. Blood pressure asymmetry, pulse deficits and the established stenoses persisted. This case suggests that normal inflammatory markers in childhood-onset Takayasu arteritis can coexist with fixed arterial damage, and that judgements about disease activity are better based on clinical findings and serial imaging together than on acute-phase reactants alone.

items.title: Anti-fibrillarin Positive Systemic Sclerosis Presenting With Myositis and Perimyocarditis.
items.abstract: A 45-year-old man with no significant past medical history presented with six months of progressive proximal muscle weakness, inflammatory arthralgia, and functional decline, on a background of two years of progressive depigmented pruritic skin lesions. Examination demonstrated widespread hypopigmented sclerotic skin changes, sclerodactyly, and digital ulceration. Investigations revealed mildly elevated creatine kinase (CK) and cardiac biomarkers, with cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrating perimyocarditis and thigh MRI showing symmetrical muscle oedema consistent with inflammatory myopathy. Skin biopsy demonstrated dermal fibrosis while serology was positive for anti-fibrillarin antibodies. A diagnosis of anti-fibrillarin-positive systemic sclerosis with inflammatory myositis was made. Treatment with low-dose prednisolone and colchicine resulted in clinical improvement, with mycophenolate mofetil (MMF) planned as a steroid-sparing agent. Initiation was delayed following a positive QuantiFERON-TB (QIAGEN GmbH, Hilden, Germany) test requiring management of latent tuberculosis (TB). This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of anti-fibrillarin-positive systemic sclerosis presenting with simultaneous muscular and cardiac involvement and emphasises the importance of early recognition of multisystem disease.

items.title: Beyond Xerostomia: A Two-Year Follow-Up Case Report of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Health in Primary Sjögren Syndrome.
items.abstract: Primary Sjögren syndrome (pSS) is an autoimmune disorder characterized by chronic salivary gland dysfunction that predisposes patients to oral complications and tooth loss. Although dental implant therapy has demonstrated favorable survival rates in patients with pSS, evidence regarding long-term peri-implant soft tissue health remains limited. This report describes the diagnosis of pSS following implant rehabilitation and highlights the impact of the disease on peri-implant health during a two-year follow-up. A 61-year-old man underwent implant placement at sites 14 and 16 with simultaneous sinus floor elevation and connective tissue grafting. Several months later, he developed progressive xerostomia, xerophthalmia, burning mouth symptoms, and dysphagia. Histopathological examination of a minor labial salivary gland biopsy revealed focal lymphocytic sialadenitis (Chisholm and Mason grade 3), with findings considered compatible with Sjögren syndrome in the clinical context. Following rheumatologic management with hydroxychloroquine and pilocarpine, the patient was monitored for two years. Clinical examination demonstrated persistent xerostomia and generalized gingival and peri-implant mucosal inflammation, whereas radiographic evaluation showed stable peri-implant bone levels without marginal bone loss. This case supports current evidence indicating that implant osseointegration and short-term survival can be maintained in patients with pSS despite chronic hyposalivation. However, it also illustrates that persistent salivary dysfunction and immune dysregulation may predispose peri-implant tissues to mucosal inflammation in the absence of radiographic bone loss, emphasizing that peri-implant tissue health should be evaluated independently of implant survival. Dental implants appear to represent a reliable rehabilitation option for patients with pSS when combined with individualized supportive care. Nevertheless, long-term success should be assessed not only by implant survival and marginal bone stability but also by careful monitoring of peri-implant soft tissue health. Early recognition of Sjögren syndrome by dental practitioners and multidisciplinary management are essential for optimizing both systemic and implant-related outcomes.

items.title: Digital gangrene in systemic sclerosis: prevalence, associated factors and all-cause mortality in a hospitalized cohort from southern China.
items.abstract: To investigate the cohort-specific prevalence of and factors associated with digital gangrene at baseline in systemic sclerosis (SSc), and to evaluate the incidence of gangrene and the association of baseline gangrene with all-cause mortality during follow-up. This retrospective cohort included consecutive hospitalized SSc patients (2019-2024) fulfilling 2013 ACR/EULAR criteria. Logistic regression was used to evaluate factors associated with gangrene ever at baseline. For follow-up analyses, exploratory univariable Cox regression was used to assess factors associated with incident gangrene, while multivariable Cox regression evaluated the association between gangrene ever and all-cause mortality. Of 395 patients at baseline, 41 (10.4%) had gangrene ever and 100 (25.3%) had digital ulcers (DUs) ever. In multivariable logistic regression, DUs ever (OR 21.63, 95% CI 9.32-58.20) and age (OR 1.05 per year, 95% CI 1.01-1.09) were independently associated with gangrene. Among 334 patients at risk (median follow-up 2.0 years), 10 (3.0%) developed incident gangrene (1.24 per 100 patient-years). In exploratory univariable Cox analyses, prior gangrene, DUs ever and DUs at baseline were associated with incident gangrene. During a median 2.08-year follow-up among 356 patients, 82 deaths (23.0%) occurred. In multivariable Cox analysis, gangrene ever did not show a clear independent association with all-cause mortality. In this hospitalized SSc cohort, DUs ever were strongly associated with gangrene. Furthermore, prior gangrene and DUs identified patients at higher risk for subsequent gangrene events. However, gangrene ever did not show a clear independent association with all-cause mortality.

items.title: Applicability of metabolomics in axial spondyloarthritis: a scoping review.
items.abstract: This scoping review aims to explore the applicability of metabolomics in identifying biomarkers for early diagnosis and disease monitoring in patients with axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA). We conducted a scoping review following the PRISMA-ScR and JBI guidelines. Searches were carried out on the Web of Science, Scopus, and MEDLINE databases. After applying the eligibility criteria, 13 articles were included in the final analysis. Specific metabolic signatures, mainly amino acid, fatty acid, and energy and lipid metabolism metabolites, were identified as potential tools for distinguishing axSpA patients from healthy controls and assessing treatment response. Metabolomics holds considerable promise for advancing the understanding of axSpA pathophysiology and facilitating biomarker discovery. However, further validation in diverse populations and methodological standardization are required before these findings can be translated into clinical practice.

items.title: Three's (Autoimmune) Company: A Co-occurrence of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura, Warm Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia, and Sjögren's Syndrome.
items.abstract: This case highlights the successful management of atypical, refractory thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), including co-occurring autoimmune conditions, treatment-related adverse effects, and disease sequelae. A Hispanic woman in her early 50s presented to the emergency department of an academic, tertiary medical center after a syncopal episode. She reported flu-like symptoms during the preceeding 2 days. Physical examination was remarkable only for scattered ecchymoses on the upper extremities and petechiae of the lower extremities. Despite her clinical stability, she was ultimately found to have refractory TTP, warm autoimmune hemolytic anemia (wAIHA), and Sjögren's syndrome. No reports have described the co-occurrence of TTP, wAIHA, and Sjögren's syndrome. Isolated case reports have described co-occurring TTP and Sjögren's syndrome, as well as co-occurring or sequential TTP and wAIHA, with or without lupus. We report what is, to our knowledge, one of the first cases of co-occurring TTP, wAIHA, and Sjögren syndrome. This case underscores the importance of multidisciplinary care in the management of refractory TTP and its associated complications.

items.title: Catastrophic Antiphospholipid Syndrome in a Young Adult: A Case Report and Literature Review.
items.abstract: Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome (CAPS) is a rare, life-threatening variant of antiphospholipid syndrome marked by rapid multiorgan thrombosis. Early diagnosis remains challenging, especially in young adults. A 22-year-old woman with immune thrombocytopenia, Raynaud's phenomenon, and a recent cholecystectomy presented with headache, abdominal pain, and systemic symptoms. She developed thrombotic events in the brain, spleen, and kidneys. Laboratory testing demonstrated positive antiphospholipid antibodies, and renal biopsy confirmed thrombotic microangiopathy. CAPS was diagnosed in the context of evolving systemic lupus erythematosus. Treatment included corticosteroids, plasma exchange, anticoagulation, hydroxychloroquine, and rituximab. Despite delayed recognition due to overlapping autoimmune conditions, multidisciplinary management led to clinical stabilization. This case highlights the diagnostic complexity of CAPS in young patients with autoimmune comorbidities. Early recognition and aggressive multidisciplinary treatment are essential for favorable outcomes.

items.title: Higher Daily Hospitalization Costs and Intensive Care Utilization Among Decedents With Systemic Lupus Erythematosus and Rheumatoid Arthritis: A Bioethical Analysis of End-of-Life Care.
items.abstract: End-of-life care creates financial burdens. This study examines medical procedures/interventions and costs for inpatients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA), comparing those who died during hospitalization to those who survived, analyzing the findings through a bioethical perspective. This observational 1:1 case-control study was conducted at a tertiary care center. Patients with SLE and RA (ICD-10-CM diagnostic codes) who were hospitalized for at least 24 h during two distinct periods-January-June 2019 and January-June 2023-were included. Patients were designated as cases if they died during hospitalization and as controls if they were discharged alive. Data were abstracted from electronic medical records using standardized formats. Microcosting data for each hospitalization were obtained from the accounting department. We identified 29 matched pairs of cases and controls, primarily comprising middle-aged females, with SLE. Cases and controls had similar sociodemographic and disease-related characteristics. However, cases spent a greater proportion of their hospitalization time in the intensive care unit (100% [33.9-100] vs. 27.5% [13.4-45], p ≤ 0.001) and had higher incidence of complications (75.9% vs. 34.5%, p = 0.003). Daily hospitalization costs were significantly higher for cases (USD 3348 vs. 2707.4, p = < 0.001). More cases utilized blood bank services, while fewer engaged in clinical nutrition-related procedures. Decedents with SLE/RA had higher daily hospitalization costs than matched survivors, in the context of greater ICU utilization, complications, and blood bank use. End-of-life scenarios are complex; clinical decisions should be examined through bioethical lens.

items.title: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is associated with reduced levels of biochemical bone status indices reflecting altered bone formation.
items.abstract: Individuals with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) are at increased risk of impaired bone health and fractures. This prospective case-control study assessed bone mineral density (BMD) and bone and cartilage biomarkers in children with JIA and healthy controls. Fifty-one individuals with well-characterized JIA (age 1.6-17.9 years) and 61 age-matched controls from the same region were included. Joint erosions were assessed radiographically, and BMD was measured by digital X-ray radiogrammetry (DXR). Bone formation was assessed using serum intact procollagen type I N-propeptide (PINP) and bone-specific alkaline phosphatase (BALP), and bone resorption was assessed by C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX). Cartilage synthesis was assessed by serum type II procollagen C-terminal propeptide (PIICP). Biomarkers were measured at baseline and 1-year follow-up, while joint erosions were evaluated up to 5 years. Soluble urokinase plasminogen activator receptor (a.k.a. suPAR), rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, and antinuclear antibodies were also measured. The DXR Z-scores were lower in the polyarticular subtype JIA group in comparison with controls (p = 0.010). The polyarticular JIA group had lower PINP levels in comparison with controls at inclusion (p = 0.028) and after 1 year (p = 0.006). Serum BALP levels were lower in the overall JIA group and in the polyarticular group at 1 year, p = 0.031 and p = 0.042, respectively. Plasma CTX levels were lower in individuals receiving oral steroids compared with those not receiving steroid therapy (p = 0.006). Higher PIICP levels were found in the oligoarticular subtype JIA group in comparison with the control group (p = 0.020). Based on our findings, children with JIA, particularly those with polyarticular disease, are at increased risk of compromised bone health over time, potentially related to reduced bone formation. These findings underscore the importance of monitoring bone health and implementing targeted interventions to promote optimal peak bone mass acquisition in children with JIA.

items.title: Pharyngotonsillitis, aphthous stomatitis, and adenitis precede familial Mediterranean fever by two decades.
items.abstract: Familial Mediterranean fever (FMF) and periodic fever, aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis, and cervical adenitis (PFAPA) syndrome share innate-immune features, but population-level data on oropharyngeal morbidity before FMF recognition are lacking. To examine the magnitude, timing, specificity, and treatment burden of a PFAPA-like oropharyngeal phenotype in patients later diagnosed with FMF. Population-based matched case-control study in Leumit Health Services, Israel. FMF patients with colchicine dispensing (n = 3324) were matched 1:4 by birth year and sex to 13,296 controls. Oropharyngeal diagnoses, tonsil/adenoid surgery, antibiotic dispensing, and ear, nose, and throat (ENT) visits were compared across windows up to 20 and 10 years before diagnosis (30-day blackout), using streptococcal, hypertrophy, and non-ENT negative controls with false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment. A PFAPA diagnostic code was recorded in 2.6% of FMF patients versus 0.1% of controls (odds ratio [OR] 25.4, 95% confidence interval 14.3-48.5). Up to 20 years before diagnosis, future FMF patients had more acute tonsillitis (35.6% vs. 27.2%; OR 1.48, 1.37-1.61), viral-labeled tonsillitis (OR 2.65), oral aphthae (OR 1.72), and cervical lymphadenitis (OR 1.62; all q < 0.05); associations persisted after diagnosis. Streptococcal sore-throat coding was not increased (lifelong OR 1.03, 0.94-1.14). Antibiotic dispensing and ENT visits were increased; tonsillectomy alone was more frequent (OR 2.51), although surgical comparisons did not survive FDR correction. FMF is associated with a non-streptococcal, PFAPA-like oropharyngeal phenotype detectable years before diagnosis. Recurrent pharyngotonsillitis with aphthae or cervical adenitis, without demonstrated streptococcal disease, may be a clinical cue to consider FMF in at-risk populations.

items.title: Factors associated with tocilizumab primary failure in the treatment of giant cell arteritis.
items.abstract: Giant cell arteritis (GCA) is the most common systemic vasculitis in adults over 50. Tocilizumab (TCZ), the first biologic approved in GCA, enables glucocorticoid-sparing remission, but reliable predictors of treatment outcome at initiation are lacking. We aimed to identify baseline and follow-up predictors of TCZ failure in GCA. In this retrospective single-centre cohort study, consecutive GCA patients receiving their first TCZ course at Caen University Hospital (2014-2024) were included, excluding early withdrawal (<3 months). Two multivariable logistic regression models were built using backward stepwise elimination: a baseline model and a combined baseline-and-follow-up model incorporating FDG-PET/CT metabolic response. Of 91 patients, TCZ was successful in 43 (47%) and failed in 48 (53%). Baseline multivariable analysis identified three predictors of failure: CRP > 63.5 mg/L (OR 3.40; 95% CI 1.26-9.77; P<0.05), large-vessel vasculitis (LVV; OR 3.22; 95% CI 1.18-9.44; P<0.05) and previous relapse before TCZ (OR 3.75; 95% CI 1.16-9.41; P<0.05). A predictive score yielded an AUC of 0.774 (95% CI 0.674-0.873). In the combined follow-up model, PET/CT extinction status was significantly associated with treatment outcome overall (P<0.001). A longer duration of TCZ exposure was associated with a lower risk of failure (OR 0.911 per additional month, 95% CI 0.822-0.997; P<0.05). Baseline CRP, LVV and prior relapses can be combined into a simple predictive score to stratify the probability of TCZ response in GCA. Complete metabolic extinction on FDG-PET/CT during treatment further identifies patients at risk of failure.

items.title: Nano-Armor Empowers Mesenchymal Stem Cells to Actively Target and Reverse Synovial Inflammation in Rheumatoid Arthritis.
items.abstract: Mesenchymal stem cell (MSC) therapy for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) remains hindered by the oxidative-induced pro-inflammatory synovial microenvironment, which largely impairs MSC homing, survival, and immunomodulatory function. Although nanomaterial modification holds promise for enhancing MSC therapeutic efficacy, conventional intracellular modification approaches carry risks of cytotoxicity and unpredictable stem cell fate alteration. Here, we empower MSCs with a surface-anchored, multifunctional RGD-MXene/MnO₂ nano-armor (RMM). MXene, with its large specific surface area, supports the in-situ growth of MnO₂ nanozymes and conjugation of RGD targeting peptides, while enabling stable covalent anchoring onto the MSC membrane via click chemistry. The RMM-armored MSCs exhibit robust protection against ROS-induced damage and fully restored immunomodulatory capacity due to the cascade catalase- and superoxide dismutase-like activities of MnO 2 , efficiently promoting macrophage polarization from pro-inflammatory M1 type to anti-inflammatory M2 type. In RA mouse models, the RGD peptide facilitates active MSC homing to inflamed synovial tissues by specifically recognizing integrin αvβ3. Thus, RMM@MSCs not only alleviate synovial inflammation but also prevent bone destruction and cartilage erosion, achieving highly efficient RA therapy with only one dose. This surface modification strategy resolves the long-standing translational barriers of conventional MSC therapy, providing a versatile and translatable platform for treating RA and other inflammatory diseases. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Although mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) are promising for rheumatoid arthritis (RA) due to their inherent immunomodulatory properties, their translation is hindered by poor homing to inflammatory joints and ROS-induced functional impairment. This work reports the use of a multifunctional RGD-MXene/MnO 2 (RMM) nano-armor to enhance MSC therapy in RA. Specifically, MXene provides a large specific surface area for the in-situ growth of MnO 2 nanoenzyme and the peptide conjugation, as well as the covalent anchoring on MSCs (favoring safe surface modification); MnO 2 's cascade enzyme-like activity establishes an antioxidant shield to reverse ROS-induced MSC apoptosis and exhaustion (maintaining MSC viability and biofunctions); RGD peptide targets highly expressed integrin αvβ3 in synovial pannus (enabling active MSC homing). Thus, the nano-armor-modified RMM@MSCs significantly inhibits synovitis, alleviates symptoms, and mitigates joint destruction.

items.title: Study outcomes for eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis and hypereosinophilic syndrome: towards achieving treatment goals in clinical practice.
items.abstract: Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis (EGPA) and hypereosinophilic syndrome (HES) are rare systemic inflammatory conditions associated with eosinophilia and end-organ damage. Therapeutic aims for these diseases should include achieving sustained remission, preventing relapse, minimizing disease and treatment-related organ damage, restoring and maintaining quality of life and reducing mortality. To achieve these treatment goals in clinical practice, there is a need for clearly defined clinical outcomes, in addition to early diagnosis to facilitate early therapeutic intervention. This narrative review examines how clinical outcomes are currently defined and assessed in EGPA and HES studies and discusses how related treatment goals can be achieved, including the challenges physicians may face when implementing them. Treatment comparisons between studies are complicated by differences in how treatment-related outcomes are defined. Remission and relapse outcomes are generally well reported, although heterogeneously defined, while treatment-free remission, treatment-related toxicity, target-organ damage, mortality and patient-reported outcomes require further study. Additionally, many assessment tools utilized in clinical research are unreliable, not standardized and/or not disease-specific. Consensus definitions of treatment goals and disease-specific desired outcomes would facilitate better assessment and comparison of treatment responses in clinical practice for both EGPA and HES, supporting clinicians to set ambitious and achievable treatment goals for their patients. items.title: Receptor-Guided Nanomedicine for Rheumatoid Arthritis: Linking Target Biology, Nanocarrier Design, and Translation.
items.abstract: Rheumatoid arthritis (RA) is a chronic autoimmune disease characterized by persistent synovitis and progressive joint destruction. Although current therapies improve disease control, inadequate lesion selectivity, heterogeneous responses, and systemic toxicity remain important limitations. Receptor-guided nanomedicine offers a strategy to align drug delivery with disease-relevant cell populations and pathological processes. This Review examines how receptor biology and pharmacological characteristics shape ligand selection, carrier architecture, payload choice, administration route, and microenvironment-responsive design in RA nanotherapy. Particular emphasis is placed on folate receptor-β (FRβ) and CD44, which represent the most extensively investigated receptor axes for activated macrophages and broader synovial cell populations, respectively. Representative platforms delivering antirheumatic drugs, glucocorticoids, natural products, nucleic acids, and functional nanomaterials are comparatively analyzed, while emerging targets including scavenger receptors, Fc gamma receptor I, pattern-recognition receptors, and integrin αvβ3 are discussed in their pathological contexts. Key translational issues, including receptor heterogeneity, target validation, formulation complexity, long-term safety, manufacturability, and patient stratification, are highlighted. Linking target biology with nanocarrier design may support more rational development of receptor-guided nanomedicines for RA.

items.title: [Underestimated Risk in Ankylosing Spondylitis: Iatrogenic Thoracic Spine Fracture During Revision Hip Arthroplasty With Fatal Outcome].
items.abstract: Spinal fractures in advanced ankylosing spondylitis (AS) are highly unstable. Their iatrogenic occurrence during extra-articular revision hip arthroplasty is extremely rare. We report on an 81-year-old AS patient who sustained an unnoticed thoracic type C fracture (T8/9) due to forced reduction maneuvers during revision total hip arthroplasty. Postoperatively, the patient developed acute paraplegia and passed away shortly after due to neuro-cardiopulmonary failure. In patients with a rigid spine, forced femoral manipulation transfers severe shear forces via the pelvis directly to the thoracic spine. Recognition of clinical red flags, protective positioning, and interdisciplinary SOPs are mandatory to prevent this fatal complication. Wirbelsäulenfrakturen bei ankylosierender Spondylitis (AS, Morbus Bechterew) sind aufgrund der rigiden, ankylosierten Wirbelsäule biomechanisch hochinstabil und häufig mit schweren neurologischen Defiziten assoziiert. Das Auftreten einer solchen Fraktur im Rahmen nicht-spinaler orthopädischer Eingriffe, insbesondere während einer Hüftrevisionsendoprothetik, ist äußerst selten.Wir berichten über einen 81-jährigen Patienten mit fortgeschrittener AS und rezidivierenden Luxationen einer Hüfttotalendoprothese. Im Rahmen einer auswärtigen Revisionsoperation erfolgte ein Wechsel von Femurschaft und Kopf. Aufgrund der ankylosierten Wirbelsäule war die Lagerung erschwert; während der Reposition wurde ein Knackgeräusch wahrgenommen. Postoperativ entwickelte der Patient starke Rückenschmerzen, eine akute Paraplegie sowie eine Blasen- und Mastdarmstörung. Die MRT zeigte eine grob dislozierte thorakale Typ-C-Zerreißungsfraktur auf Höhe Th8/9. Es erfolgte die notfallmäßige dorsale Stabilisierung von Th4 bis L1 mit Reposition und Dekompression. Trotz technisch erfolgreicher Stabilisierung kam es wenige Stunden später zum Kreislaufkollaps mit letalem Ausgang. Die Obduktion ergab eine schwere thorakale Rückenmarksschädigung mit zentraler Regulationsstörung, Hirnödem und kardio-pulmonaler Dekompensation.Der Fall verdeutlicht eine seltene, aber potenziell fatale Komplikation der Hüftrevisionsendoprothetik bei AS. Präoperative Erkennung ankylosierter Wirbelsäulen, angepasste Lagerung, vorsichtige Repositionsmanöver und interdisziplinäre SOPs sind zentrale präventive Maßnahmen.
